items.title: 22.6.1 Reactions of the -OH Group in Phenols

source_refs.note: Topic 22.6.1, printed pages 92-93 (PDF 95-96), with the book's schemes as diagrams and their corrections; 'an ether is produced' is marked (the product is an ester).

blocks.text: The -OH group in phenols has a slightly acidic character It can therefore act as an acid and take part in acid-base reactions.

Phenols are only slightly soluble in water due to the large non-polar benzene ring. However, they do dissolve in alkaline solutions and undergo acid-base reactions with bases to form a soluble salt and water.

blocks.alt: Phenol (labelled acid), a benzene ring with OH, + NaOH (labelled base) gives sodium phenoxide, the ring with O- Na+, + H2O. Labels: phenol, sodium hydroxide, sodium phenoxide.
blocks.caption: i) Phenol and sodium hydroxide (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 95).

blocks.text: Molten phenols react vigorously with reactive metals such as sodium (Na). This is also an acid-base reaction. Now, a soluble salt is formed and hydrogen gas is given off.

blocks.alt: 2 phenol + 2Na gives 2 sodium phenoxide (ring with O- Na+) + H2. Labels: phenol, sodium, sodium phenoxide.
blocks.caption: ii) Phenol and sodium (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 95).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed equation has one phenol + 2Na on the left but 2 sodium phenoxide on the right, so it is not balanced; it is drawn as 2 phenol + 2Na -> 2 sodium phenoxide + H2.

When phenol is heated with acyl chloride in the presence of a base, an ether is produced. The base is needed to deprotonate the phenol and form a phenoxide ion. The phenoxide ion is a better nucleophile than the original phenol molecule and will be able to attack the carbonyl carbon.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The product, phenyl ethanoate (CH₃COOC₆H₅), is an ester, not an ether, as the book's own equation shows.

blocks.alt: Displayed ethanoyl chloride, CH3-C(=O)-Cl, + phenol, HO-C6H5, with NaOH over the arrow and Heat under it, gives phenyl ethanoate, CH3-C(=O)-O-C6H5, + HCl. Labels: ethanoyl chloride, phenol, phenyl ethanoate.
blocks.caption: iii) Ethanoyl chloride and phenol to phenyl ethanoate (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 96).

blocks.alt: A hydroxide ion uses a lone pair (curly arrow) to take the H of phenol's O-H group, and a second curly arrow moves the O-H bond electrons onto the O. The arrow gives the phenoxide ion, labelled 'better nucleophile than the phenol', + H2O.
blocks.caption: Phenol and hydroxide ion to the phenoxide ion (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 96).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed sketch leaves out the water formed when OH- removes the proton; + H2O is added above.
This reaction of phenol will be discussed in Chapter 24 (Organic Nitrogen Compounds).
